summary: Proposes optional extensions to POP3 so a workstation can read messages from a discussion group server in the same way it reads from a mailbox server. It builds on the earlier POP3 memo. Every extension it describes is optional, and the memo asks for discussion.

eli5.summary: Besides your own mailbox, you may want to read a big group chat board. This adds extra ways for the same mail-fetching tool to read that board too.

questions: how to read news groups with pop3
subtitle: Add discussion group mailbox access to POP3 so one client can read both personal mail and shared group messages.

tldr.problem: Discussion groups are traditionally replicated to every subscribing host, wasting disk space and bandwidth, or kept central but forcing users to log into a separate host. A better approach keeps groups on a central server but allows remote access.
tldr.mechanism: POP3 is extended with an XTND command that lets clients open and browse discussion group mailboxes the same way they access personal mail, with metadata tracking the last message retrieved.
tldr.outcome: Multiple users at one site can share a single copy of discussion group mail, accessed remotely through the same POP3 client that handles personal mail.

facts.label: List format
facts.value: NAME MAXIMA (and optionally SIZE for messages)

today: RFC 1082 is Unknown status and has not been obsoleted. The POP3 extensions for discussion groups were implemented and used successfully in some systems, particularly in the MH message handling system. However, they remained optional and never became a widespread standard. Modern systems typically use specialized protocols for mailing lists and newsgroups, such as NNTP or web-based forums.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content:
Discussion groups (also called interest groups or bulletin boards) connect subscribers with a common interest. Members post messages to a distribution address, and the mail system sends copies to all subscribers. This simple model has problems at sites with multiple hosts and many subscribers.

The traditional solutions both have drawbacks. Replication stores a complete copy of each discussion group on every host, wasting gigabytes of disk space and forcing network redundancy. Centralization keeps messages on a single host but forces users to log into that host in addition to their local machine, which is inconvenient. POP3 already lets workstations access personal mail from a central mailbox server; this RFC extends POP3 so clients can also access discussion group mailboxes the same way.

The memo assumes familiarity with RFC 1081 (Post Office Protocol Version 3) and describes optional extensions to enable discussion group mail delivery and retrieval.
sections.eli5: There's a big mailbox at the office with messages everyone in your team should read. Rather than copying the whole thing to your desk, you want to check it the same way you check your own mailbox.

sections.title: Discussion Group Concepts
sections.content:
Discussion groups are formally described by seven parameters. The name is a token like unix-wizards (case-insensitive). Aliases are shorter local alternatives. The address is the distribution address (e.g., Unix-Wizards@BRL.MIL). The request address reaches the group moderator, who manages subscriptions and archive decisions.

The maxima is a special number that increases by at least one each time a message arrives, never decreasing. It serves as a magic cookie; clients can detect new messages by checking if the current maxima is higher than the last one they saw. The last date is the timestamp of the last message received. These two values allow efficient polling: a client can determine if new messages exist without listing all messages.

Discussion groups often use an exploder, an agent that expands a single address to the full subscriber list and redirects error reports to the moderator instead of the message sender. This reduces noise for senders and helps moderators maintain the subscription list.

Some sites maintain a two-level archive scheme: current messages in a standard maildrop, recent archive messages in an archive maildrop, and older messages offline. This lets a POP3 client access both current and archived discussions.
sections.eli5: Each group has a name and a boss. There's a counter that goes up every time a new message arrives. The client checks this counter to know if there's anything new to read.

sections.title: The XTND Extensions
sections.content:
All new facilities are introduced through a single POP3 command: XTND. These commands are valid only in the transaction state, after the user has logged in. They operate on discussion group mailboxes.

The XTND BBOARDS command, with no argument, lists all world-readable discussion groups on the server with their current maxima. With an argument naming a specific group, it opens that group's maildrop for reading. The command returns a multi-line response with the format NAME MAXIMA followed by optional additional information.

When a discussion group is opened via XTND BBOARDS, the normal POP3 LIST command (which usually returns MSGNO SIZE) is extended to return MSGNO SIZE MAXIMA, allowing clients to see which maxima value was assigned to each message.

The XTND ARCHIVE command opens the archive maildrop for a discussion group, allowing users to browse older messages. It requires a group name argument and returns the same multi-line listing format.

The XTND X-BBOARDS command returns detailed metadata about a group (name, aliases, address, request address, flags, and maxima) in a 14-line format. Lines 1, 2, 9, 10, 13, and 14 (name, aliases, address, request address, flags with maxima, and last date) are of general interest; the others are system-specific.

Unlike personal mailboxes where DELE removes messages, discussion group mailboxes opened via XTND are read-only to POP3 clients. The DELE command is a no-op on group mailboxes.
sections.eli5: A new command, XTND, asks the server to open a group's mailbox. You can list all groups, open a specific one, read its archive, or get detailed information about it.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes two optional policies for POP3 servers hosting discussion groups.

Private discussion groups allow administrators to restrict access. Once a user logs in via POP3, the server grants access to exactly those discussion groups the authenticated user is permitted to read. Private groups should not appear in listings from XTND BBOARDS unless the user has permission.

Anonymous POP3 access permits world-readable discussion groups to be accessed without authentication. A server can accept a USER command for anonymous (valid with any password) to let clients browse public groups. For security, administrators should limit such access to local hosts or a configured access list.

Implementation experience showed that two optimizations are critical. First, caching the metadata structures describing discussion groups in the POP3 server prevents repeated filesystem access. Second, clients should retrieve only headers and first lines when scanning listings, and retrieve full messages only when needed. This substantially improves performance, especially over slow links.
sections.eli5: Servers can make some groups private (only certain people see them) and some public (anyone can browse). They should cache group information to stay fast.

sections.title: Client Access Patterns
sections.content:
A mail client can use POP3 extensions to treat discussion groups like shared mailboxes. The client logs in once, then issues XTND BBOARDS to list available groups. For each group, it can check the current maxima and compare it to the maxima of the last message the user saw. If maxima has increased, new messages are available.

When a user wants to read a group, the client issues XTND BBOARDS with the group name to open it. The LIST command then returns messages with their assigned maxima values, allowing the client to remember where the user left off. Clients can efficiently poll for new messages by simply checking maxima changes without retrieving any messages.

The XTND ARCHIVE command lets clients switch to reading older messages without losing context. A well-designed client can seamlessly present both current and archive messages as one continuous view.

Since discussion group mailboxes are read-only from the POP3 perspective, clients do not attempt to delete or modify messages. The server handles message removal and archiving based on local policy.
sections.eli5: Your mail client asks the server what groups exist, checks if there's anything new, and switches between reading current messages and old archived ones.
